# complex translation {.divider}

We now put translation to work on complex natural language arguments.


## the plan

Three steps, applied to each argument in turn:

::: {.incremental}
1. write the argument in **premise-conclusion form**
2. **translate** the argument into the language of propositional logic
3. use a **truth table** to determine whether the argument is valid
:::



# example 1: the burglar {.divider}


## the argument

> My client is not the burglar. For several reasons. If there are no signs of forced entry, then my client is the burglar only if she had an accomplice inside. But we can discard that option, as no one in the building could have known my client before today. Nor are there any signs of forced entry.



## in premise-conclusion form

::: {.argument}
1. If there are no signs of forced entry, then my client is the burglar only if she had an accomplice inside.
2. She did not have an accomplice inside.
3. There are no signs of forced entry.

::: {.conclusion}
4. My client is not the burglar.
:::
:::


## translation key {.smaller}


We specify a **translation key**:

::: {.argument}
$p$: There are signs of forced entry.

$q$: My client is the burglar.

$r$: My client had an accomplice inside.
:::


## premise 1 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: There are signs of forced entry.

$q$: My client is the burglar.

$r$: My client had an accomplice inside.
:::
:::


```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
1. ~p -> (q -> r): If there are no signs of forced entry, then my client is the burglar only if she had an accomplice inside.
```


## premise 2 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: There are signs of forced entry.

$q$: My client is the burglar.

$r$: My client had an accomplice inside.
:::
:::


```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
2. ~r: She did not have an accomplice inside.
```


## premise 3 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: There are signs of forced entry.

$q$: My client is the burglar.

$r$: My client had an accomplice inside.
:::
:::


```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
3. ~p: There are no signs of forced entry.
```



## conclusion {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: There are signs of forced entry.

$q$: My client is the burglar.

$r$: My client had an accomplice inside.
:::
:::

```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
4. ~q: My client is not the burglar.
```

## the argument translated

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: There are signs of forced entry.

$q$: My client is the burglar.

$r$: My client had an accomplice inside.
:::
:::

::: {.argument}
1. $\neg p \to (q \to r)$
2. $\neg r$
3. $\neg p$
4. $\neg q$

::: {.conclusion}
5. $p$
:::
:::

## the question of validity

```{.TruthTable mode="validity"}
~p -> (q -> r)
~r
~p
~q
```






# example 2: mind and brain {.divider}


## the argument

> If the mind and the brain are one and the same thing, then the mind is material only if the brain is. But the mind is not material unless it is divisible. The brain is material, but the mind is not divisible. So the mind and the brain are not one and the same thing.



## in premise-conclusion form

::: {.argument}
1. If the mind and the brain are one and the same thing, then the mind is material only if the brain is.
2. The mind is not material unless it is divisible.
3. The brain is material, but the mind is not divisible.

::: {.conclusion}
4. The mind and the brain are not one and the same thing.
:::
:::


## translation key {.smaller}


We specify a **translation key**:

::: {.argument}
$p$: The mind and the brain are one and the same thing.

$q$: The mind is material.

$r$: The brain is material.

$t$: The mind is divisible.
:::


## premise 1 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: The mind and the brain are one and the same thing.

$q$: The mind is material.

$r$: The brain is material.

$t$: The mind is divisible.
:::
:::


```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
1. p -> (q -> r): If the mind and the brain are one and the same thing, then the mind is material only if the brain is.
```


## premise 2 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: The mind and the brain are one and the same thing.

$q$: The mind is material.

$r$: The brain is material.

$t$: The mind is divisible.
:::
:::


```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
2. ~t -> ~r: The mind is not material unless it is divisible.
```


## premise 3 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: The mind and the brain are one and the same thing.

$q$: The mind is material.

$r$: The brain is material.

$t$: The mind is divisible.
:::
:::


```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
3. q /\ ~t: The brain is material, but the mind is not divisible.
```



## conclusion {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: The mind and the brain are one and the same thing.

$q$: The mind is material.

$r$: The brain is material.

$t$: The mind is divisible.
:::
:::

```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
4. ~p: The mind and the brain are not one and the same thing.
```

## the argument translated

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: The mind and the brain are one and the same thing.

$q$: The mind is material.

$r$: The brain is material.

$t$: The mind is divisible.
:::
:::

::: {.argument}
1. $p \to (q \to r)$
2. $\neg t \to \neg r$
3. $q \wedge \neg t$
4. $\neg p$

::: {.conclusion}
5. $p$
:::
:::

## the question of validity

There are \\(2\^4 = 16\\) assignments.

A full truth table would require 16 rows ...

```{.TruthTable mode="validity"}
p -> (q -> r)
~t -> ~ r
q /\ ~ t
~ p
```


## search for a counterexample


We now employ the **search for a counterexample method**:

::: {.incremental}
1.  Focus on assignments that **make the conclusion false**

   
2.  Ask **which of the assignments that remain make the premises true**.
    

3.  If we **find a counterexample**, then **the argument is invalid**. 

      **Otherwise**, **the argument is valid**.

:::

##  make the conclusion false {.smaller}

To make the conclusion $\neg p$ **false**, we must have $p: T$:

$$
p : T
$$

So, we need only look at **8** rows out the 16:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
p & q & r & t &p \to (q \to r) & \neg t \to \neg r & q \wedge \neg t & \neg p \\
\hline
T & T & T & T & &  &  & \color{red}{F}  \\
T & T & T & F & &  &  & \color{red}{F} \\
T & T & F & T & &  &  & \color{red}{F} \\
T & T & F & F & &  &  & \color{red}{F} \\
T & F & T & T & &  &  & \color{red}{F} \\
T & F & T & F & &  &  & \color{red}{F} \\
T & F & F & T & &  &  & \color{red}{F} \\
T & F & F & F& &  &  & \color{red}{F} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$

## filter the candidate rows {.smaller}

To make the third premise $q \wedge \neg t$ true, we consider only rows at which 

$$
q : T \qquad t : F
$$
    This narrows down the field of potential counterexamples to two rows:


$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
p & q & r & t &p \to (q \to r) & \neg t \to \neg r & q \wedge \neg t & \neg p \\
\hline
T & T & F & T & &  & \color{red}{T}  & \color{red}{F} \\
T & T & F & F & &  & \color{red}{T} & \color{red}{F} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$


To make the second premise $\neg t \to \neg r$ true, we rule out the row at which $t$ is false and $r$ is true:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
p & q & r & t &p \to (q \to r) & \neg t \to \neg r & q \wedge \neg t & \neg p \\
\hline
T & T & F & T & & \color{red}{T} & \color{red}{T}  & \color{red}{F} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$

The row that remains **falsifies** the first premise, which means that it is **not** a counterexample to validity:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
p & q & r & t &p \to (q \to r) & \neg t \to \neg r & q \wedge \neg t & \neg p \\
\hline
T & T & F & T & F & \color{red}{T} & \color{red}{T}  & \color{red}{F} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
It follows that the argument is **valid**.


# example 3: insurance {.divider}

## the argument

> Your insurer will cover your expenses only if you are at fault or are current with your monthly payments. But if you are current with your monthly payments, then you can afford to cover the expenses yourself. So, your insurer will not cover your expenses unless you can afford to cover them yourself.


## in premise-conclusion form

::: {.argument}
1. Your insurer will cover your expenses only if you are at fault or are current with your monthly payments.
2. If you are current with your monthly payments, then you can afford to cover the expenses yourself.

::: {.conclusion}
3. Your insurer will not cover your expenses unless you can afford to cover them yourself.
:::
:::


## translation key {.smaller}


We specify a **translation key**:

::: {.argument}
$p$: Your insurer will cover your expenses.

$q$: You are at fault.

$r$: You are current with your monthly payments.

$t$: You can afford to cover the expenses yourself.
:::


## premise 1 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Your insurer will cover your expenses.

$q$: You are at fault.

$r$: You are current with your monthly payments.

$t$: You can afford to cover the expenses yourself.
:::
:::


```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
1. p -> (q \/ r): Your insurer will cover your expenses only if you are at fault or are current with your monthly payments.
```


## premise 2 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Your insurer will cover your expenses.

$q$: You are at fault.

$r$: You are current with your monthly payments.

$t$: You can afford to cover the expenses yourself.
:::
:::


```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
2. r -> t: If you are current with your monthly payments, then you can afford to cover the expenses yourself.
```





## conclusion {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Your insurer will cover your expenses.

$q$: You are at fault.

$r$: You are current with your monthly payments.

$t$: You can afford to cover the expenses yourself.
:::
:::

```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
3. ~t -> ~p: Your insurer will not cover your expenses unless you can afford to cover them yourself.
```

## the argument translated

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Your insurer will cover your expenses.

$q$: You are at fault.

$r$: You are current with your monthly payments.

$t$: You can afford to cover the expenses yourself.
:::
:::

::: {.argument}
1. $p \to (q \vee r)$
2. $r \to t$

::: {.conclusion}
3. $\neg t \to \neg p$
:::
:::

## the question of validity

There are \\(2\^4 = 16\\) assignments.

A full truth table would require 16 rows ...

```{.TruthTable mode="validity"}
p -> (q \/ r)
r -> t
~ t -> ~p
```








## search for a counterexample


We now employ the **search for a counterexample method**:

::: {.incremental}
1.  Focus on assignments that **make the conclusion false**

   
2.  Ask **which of the assignments that remain make the premises true**.
    

3.  If we **find a counterexample**, then **the argument is invalid**. 

      **Otherwise**, **the argument is valid**.

:::

##  make the conclusion false {.smaller}

To make the conclusion $\neg t \to \neg p$ **false**, we must have:

$$
t : F \qquad p : T
$$

So, we need look only at **4** rows out the 16:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
p & q & r & t &p \to (q \vee r) & r \to t & \neg t \to \neg p \\
\hline
T & T & T & F & &  &   \color{red}{F} \\
T & T & F & F & &  &   \color{red}{F} \\
T & F & T & F & &  &   \color{red}{F} \\
T & F & F & F& &  &   \color{red}{F} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$

## filter the candidate rows {.smaller}

To make the third premise $r \to t$ true, we rule out rows at which 

$$
r : T \qquad t : F
$$
    This narrows down the field of potential counterexamples to two rows:
    
  $$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
p & q & r & t &p \to (q \vee r) & r \to t & \neg t \to \neg p \\
\hline
T & T & F & F & & \color{red}{T} &   \color{red}{F} \\
T & F & F & F & & \color{red}{T} &   \color{red}{F} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
    
    
To make the first premise $p \to (q \vee r)$ true, we need only make $q$ true, which means that the first row is now a counterexample to validity:

 $$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
p & q & r & t &p \to (q \vee r) & r \to t & \neg t \to \neg p \\
\hline
T & T & F & F &  \color{red}{T} & \color{red}{T} &   \color{red}{F} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
So, we found a counterexample to validity in the assignment:
$$
p : T \qquad q : T \qquad r : F \qquad r : F
$$

It follows that the argument is **invalid**.






# example 4: the Argus deal {.divider}

Here is an argument adapted from W. O. Quine's *Methods of Logic*.

## the argument

> If Jones is ill or Smith is away, then unless Robinson comes to his senses, neither will the Argus deal be concluded nor will the directors declare a dividend. Consequently, if Smith is away and Robinson does not come to his senses, the Argus deal will not be concluded.



## in premise-conclusion form

::: {.argument}
1. If Jones is ill or Smith is away, then unless Robinson comes to his senses, neither will the Argus deal be concluded nor will the directors declare a dividend.

::: {.conclusion}
2. If Smith is away and Robinson does not come to his senses, then the Argus deal will not be concluded.
:::
:::



## translation key {.smaller}


We specify a **translation key**:

::: {.argument}
$p$: Jones is ill.

$q$: Smith is away.

$r$: Robinson comes to his senses.

$t$: The Argus deal will be concluded.

$s$: The directors will declare a dvidend.
:::


## premise 1 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Jones is ill.

$q$: Smith is away.

$r$: Robinson comes to his senses.

$t$: The Argus deal will be concluded.

$s$: The directors will declare a dvidend.
:::
:::


```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
1. (p \/ q) -> (~r -> (~t /\ ~s)): If Jones is ill or Smith is away, then unless Robinson comes to his senses, neither will the Argus deal be concluded nor will the directors declare a dividend.
```



## conclusion {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Jones is ill.

$q$: Smith is away.

$r$: Robinson comes to his senses.

$t$: The Argus deal will be concluded.

$s$: The directors will declare a dvidend.
:::
:::

```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
5. (q /\ ~r) -> ~t: If Smith is away and Robinson does not come to his senses, then the Argus deal will not be concluded.
```

## the argument translated

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Jones is ill.

$q$: Smith is away.

$r$: Robinson comes to his senses.

$t$: The Argus deal will be concluded.

$s$: The directors will declare a dvidend.
:::
:::

::: {.argument}
1. $(p \vee q) \to (\neg r \to (\neg t \wedge \neg s) )$

::: {.conclusion}
5. $(q \wedge \neg r) \to \neg t$
:::
:::



## the question of validity

There are \\(2\^5 = 32\\) assignments.

A full truth table would require 32 rows!

```{.TruthTable mode="validity"}
(p \/ q) -> (~r -> (~t /\ ~s))
(q /\ ~r) -> ~t
```


## search for a counterexample


We now employ the **search for a counterexample method**:

::: {.incremental}
1.  Focus on assignments that **make the conclusion false**

   
2.  Ask **which of the assignments that remain make the premises true**.
    

3.  If we **find a counterexample**, then **the argument is invalid**. 

      **Otherwise**, **the argument is valid**.

:::

##  make the conclusion false {.smaller}

To make the conclusion $(q \wedge \neg r) \to \neg t$ **false**, we must have:

$$
q : T \qquad r : F \qquad s : T
$$

So, we need look only at **4** rows out the 32:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
p & q & r & t & s & (p \vee q) \to (\neg r \to (\neg t \wedge \neg s) ) & (q \wedge \neg r) \to \neg t \\
\hline 
T & T & F & T & T &  &   \color{red}{F} \\
T & T & F & F & T &  &   \color{red}{F} \\
F & T & F & T & T &  &   \color{red}{F} \\
F & T & F & F & T &  &   \color{red}{F} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$

## filter the candidate rows {.smaller}

We want to make the first premise $(p \vee q) \to (\neg r \to (\neg t \wedge \neg s) )$ true. Unfortunately:

- $p \vee q$ comes out true in all four rows, and
- $\neg r \to (\neg t \wedge \neg s)$ comes out false in all four rows. 

So, the first premise comes out false in **all rows that remain.**



$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
p & q & r & t & s & (p \vee q) \to (\neg r \to (\neg t \wedge \neg s) ) & (q \wedge \neg r) \to \neg t \\
\hline 
T & T & F & T & T & F &   \color{red}{F} \\
T & T & F & F & T & F &   \color{red}{F} \\
F & T & F & T & T & F &   \color{red}{F} \\
F & T & F & F & T & F &   \color{red}{F} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$


It follows that the argument is **valid**.
